demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Rafiq Ahmed, an 80-year-old widowed South Asian man and retired Coast Guard officer, came to treatment carrying a story he had spent decades trying not to tell. When he was younger, on a coastal rescue operation, he misjudged a situation near rough water and accidentally caused serious injury to another man. In the years since, the event has never settled into a single clear narrative for him. He remembers it in disconnected pieces: the glare off the water, the slap of waves against the hull, a shout cut off by the siren, the look on the injured man's face, and then blank stretches that refuse to line up when he tries to think about it deliberately. Yet when the memory comes back, it arrives with the force of being there again, complete and immediate across all his senses, as if salt water were in his mouth and the siren were rising beside his ear.

Certain moments in daily life still pull him straight into that experience. A siren in the distance can make him freeze in his chair before he knows what has happened, and walking through a natural setting that resembles the place of the accident-shoreline paths, marshland, open water-can make his body tense and his thoughts race. Even talk about the future unsettles him; when family or friends ask about plans, he feels the ground shift beneath him, as if any forward look risks bringing the past back into view. In those moments he becomes convinced he has to be on guard all the time. He scans for danger, chooses where to sit based on how protected he feels, and avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot assess what might happen there. What frightened him most was not only the original injury but the sense that danger can appear without warning and that he may be incapable of recognizing it in time.

Those same moments also sharpen his self-judgment. When the sirens, the water, or talk of what lies ahead stir him up, he does not only feel alarm; he also becomes sure that there is something wrong with him as a person and that the accident happened because of the sort of man he is. He has come to believe that a careless or flawed part of him caused what happened, and that belief gives each trigger a moral sting. The shore, the siren, even ordinary conversations about tomorrow can feel like proof that he is still marked by the event.

To manage this, Rafiq has relied on habits that have narrowed his life. He tries to push the memories out of his mind, forcing himself toward positive thoughts and telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad. When the memory breaks through anyway, he treats it as something dangerous that must be shoved away again. This effort, however, leaves the images less settled and more fragmentary; the more he suppresses them, the more they return in flashes rather than a coherent story, and the sensory immediacy of those flashes makes the danger feel current. That sharpened sense of threat feeds back into his belief that he is defective and blameworthy, and it makes the same places and topics feel even more charged. It also pushes him to avoid unfamiliar places, to keep to routes and settings he can control, and at times to take unnecessary risks in ordinary tasks, as if proving to himself he is still capable of managing danger even while fearing it. He notices that after he has spent a day fighting thoughts, his mind seems even more likely to catch on a siren or a stretch of open water, and the old scene returns with less warning.

Over time, this pattern has shaped his retirement and his relationships. He has become more guarded in daily life, less willing to accept invitations, and more likely to sit near exits or in spots that feel protected. He lives with the sense that the world is unpredictable and that his own character is at fault for what happened long ago. Only recently, after a close family member noticed how much he startles, withdraws, and seems trapped by his own rules, did he agree to seek help. Rafiq says he is not sure he can ever fully trust himself again, but he is hoping to understand why the memory still feels so alive and whether he can stop living as though every siren, shoreline, or conversation about tomorrow is warning him that the past is about to return.
